Title: RFC: A problematic situation with the new tournament rules regarding deals

Messages.Author: Johannes Walch
Messages.Body:
Please make some comments on the following situation.

In a tournament game there are three Players left (names are fictional):
Erol, Johannes and Andreas.

Erol has allready ousted his two preys, he is now the predator of
Johannes who is the predator of Andreas. Johannes is in a bad shape
(only 2 pool) but can kill the remaining two minions of Erol with his
Shambling Hordes. If he does this Andreas will win the game. Now Erol is
offering a deal to Johannes:

"If you dont kill my minions I back-bleed Andreas and we oust him
together. In the moment before he dies you get yourself to 1 pool and
tap all your minions. You get 1 VP and I win the game."

It is a valid deal since Johannes can honor his loosing deal as long as
they are 3 and with 7 (1+6 for the oust) pool and no untapped minion he
will not stay 1 round against Erol´s 3 S&B minions.

Problem is Andreas cannot offer a counter-deal (e.g 1 for Andreas and 2
for Johannes) to Johannes because they are not allow to keep their deal
when Erol is ousted. Also Johannes practically has to accept the (worse)
Deal because that is maximizing his VPs. I consider it a very unfair
situation for Andreas because the rules don´t allow him to gain any VPs.

In my opinion the current incarnation of the rules regarding deals is
faulty and should be replaced by a more simple solution. Either don´t
have VP deals at all or don´t regulate them at all (as before). I prefer
the latter for many reasons allready stated. You?

Johannes

btw: this situation has really happened.

Messages.Author: Ben Swainbank
Messages.Body:
On May 21, 10:06 am, Johannes Walch <johannes.wa...@vekn.de> wrote:
> Please make some comments on the following situation.
>

Let's see if I have this right. We have...

A -- Dem stealth beed, 2VP
B -- Shambling Hordes, 2 pool
C -- Unknown

It's B's turn. He can smash A's minions. We're meant to feel bad for C
because B can offer A a roll-over deal of sorts, and C can't.

This is a travesty of justice. The no roll-over rule should be
scrapped.

Did I miss anything?

My Comments:

It not clear why B is offering a split deal at all. Why not just smash
A, and use the no-predator-time to go after C. Go for 2-3 VP instead
of 1. Does C have combat defense? Does B have deck that can't oust his
prey?

Let's say, C has combat defense. B needs A to back-oust his prey for
him. Why does it have to be split deal? Why can't B tell A to back-
oust C or get smashed? But wait, if A does back-oust C, won't B untap
and smash A during his turn?

And why does C have to be silent in all this? You act like a roll-over
deal is the only kind of deal there is. C can offer to rescue A's
minions if he declines B's offer. C can offer to tap out bleeding A if
B does the smashing...

In all cases, I don't see where letting players make roll-over deals,
even in your hand-picked scenario, makes the world a better place for
V:tes players.

Disalowing the endgame split forces the players to consider the table
dynamics, the end game table state, and relative capabilities of the
players and their decks. It's called playing the game.

-Ben Swainbank

There is no rule against *being* stupid. There are rules against

Unenforcable?

Keep in mind when offering such deals:

1) You must trust your deal-mate to be honorable enough to keep the
end-game deal.
2) You must trust your deal-mate to be dishonorable enough to cheat at
the game to do so.
3) You must make this "nudge-wink" illegal deal in front of a third
player, whom you are actively conspiring against.
4) The Judge does not have "prove" anything. The Judge is obligated to
apply his judgement, and apply penalties as appropriate.

-Ben Swainbank

Messages.Author: Daneel
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 21 May 2007 16:06:05 +0200, Johannes Walch
<johanne...@vekn.de> wrote:

> Problem is Andreas cannot offer a counter-deal (e.g 1 for Andreas and 2
> for Johannes) to Johannes because they are not allow to keep their deal
> when Erol is ousted. Also Johannes practically has to accept the (worse)
> Deal because that is maximizing his VPs. I consider it a very unfair

> situation for Andreas because the rules donĂ‚Â´t allow him to gain any
> VPs.

In my opinion the problem is that players can practically kill themselves
to have no chance in the endgame, thus violating the spirit of the rules
without breaking the letter.

Possible fix 1: If a deal results in a 2-player game, then it can only be
enacted in a way that both players actually try to win the game, and
secure at least a reasonable chance for the endgame (as appropriate to
the situation - but definitely not taking any specific actions solely
to diminish their chances to win in the endgame).

Possible fix 2: Players in a "lost" position (e.g. with no reasonable
chance to score any more VPs) don't count towards the number of players
when determining whether the game is 2-player or 3+-player. Thus, if one
of the players in a 3-way have no chance to win, then no VP-deals can be
made.

Possible fix 2+1: As #2 above, except that the consequences of the deal
are also considered (e.g. if the deal puts someone in a lost position,
they don't count). Thus, if one of the players in a 3-way would be hosed
by the deal so that he will no longer have any chance to win, then the
deal cannot be made (as if the table was already a 2-player table).

Not sure any of these work or are enforceable in practice, but at least
they are simple. :)

--
Regards,

Daneel

OK. So what _is_ the actual problem, here? I suppose the VP deal
is counter to the spirit of the play-to-win rules but there is a limit to
how perfect they can be. The only one who is disadvantaged by this is
Andreas. And Erol does _not_ win the game, BTW. The game would
wind up a 2-2-1 split with no game win, if I understood the above
discription.

> Problem is Andreas cannot offer a counter-deal (e.g 1 for Andreas and 2 for Johannes) to Johannes because they are not allow to

I'm not sure how anything can be charactized as "unfair" in multiplayer
games. Is it fair that Erol has been working on ousting Johannes and
wasn't given the chance because his predator and grand-predator collapsed
to Andreas too quickly? What hell is the definition of "fair" except playing
by the spirit and letter of the rules. If this leads to a relative advantage for
Erol in this situation, so be it. If you can suggest a different set of rules
to regulate these matters, fine - but you have to show how your rules would
be superior to the existing rules.

> In my opinion the current incarnation of the rules regarding deals is faulty and should be replaced by a more simple solution.
> Either don´t have VP deals at all or don´t regulate them at all (as before). I prefer the latter for many reasons allready stated.
> You?

This is where you're losing me. As others have pointed out, "Don't have
VP deals at all" sounds 'simple' but there would need to be a whole set
of protocols around it to prevent it from becoming a sham. And the protocols
you would have to set up would be anything but 'simple'. Don't regulate
them at all has it's problems, as well. I'm not saying there aren't pros and
cons to both sides, but I don't see how your example above is any worse
than the stuff that happened when VP deals were unregulated. (Well,
'unregulated' is a bad description. They were regulated; they were just
rather liberal when a player could show he had no hope of gaining a game
win.)

> btw: this situation has really happened.

We guessed.

Fred

I agree that this is a problem, but I think in reality it's only a
minor one. In the example cited, Johannes puts himself at 1 pool
BEFORE ousting his prey. Many players in Erol's situation would
simply break the deal and oust Johannes, followed by his new prey

benefits it provides to creating a game that's much more "kill your
prey to win" and less table splits.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <f2u2kf$mp2$1...@news01.versatel.de>, Johannes Walch
<johanne...@vekn.de> writes:
>James Coupe schrieb:

>> This is a better situation than before. It's not perfect. If you
>>have
>> a better suggestion, please feel free to detail it, how it would work,
>> and what up and downsides you think it would have.
>
>Why is it better than before? This is based on the assumption that
>rollover deals are bad? Why are they bad?

As can be seen from changes like banning Succubus Club, Dramatic
Upheavel, and Kindred Restructure, and from Garfield's own writing on
V:TES, the inherent structure of the game *should* be that I kill my
prey, you kill yours.

For example, Garfield expressly turned down the idea of a cross-table
oust giving me (the ouster) pool and a VP (one, the other, or both), in
favour of them going to the predator as normal. Why? Because if I have
an incentive to oust you, it should be distinct from your predator's
incentive. Perhaps, for example, you're playing an Anson Many Masters
decks, and I *really* need to bring out my copy of Anson. So I'm
willing to help oust you. Or, at least, burn Anson in some way. This
may be a strategic error on my part, but I think it's the best way -
and, if there is any dispute, the judge agrees I'm not being a complete
cock.

When I can legitimately work with a rollover deal with someone else,
this can lead to a number of problems. For example, instead of having
one predator, you have two - your real predator, and me. This causes
problems, because most of the game is set up based around the idea that
it will be your predator and prey doing nasty things to you - the
default bleed affects your prey, the undirected political action can be
blocked by predator and prey, and I can block my predator's and prey's
actions, and so on. I'm not, in general, supposed to be taking on two
Methuselahs at once.

Note that this is distinct from being the threat on the table (and so we
oust you to allow either of us to get a GW, instead of you rolling the
table). Rollover deals do not need anyone else to look like the threat.

The problem is that when I can make legitimate rollover deals, we two
stop having distinct motives. My motives are the same as my ally's
motives, and the game is not supposed to be set up that way, save for in
the most degenerate cases, which are generally but not universally
avoided.

On a simpler, though more instinctual, level, this is often regarded as
more "sporting" - attempting to win by playing the game as it was
"meant" to be played.

Going on to your "unfair" comment at the bottom - what's "fair" about
having two Methuselahs with identical motives eating me? If their
motives are absolutely identical, I have no maneuvering room to offer a
counter-deal, or openings to exploit tactically, or whatever.

>Also keep in mind that the new rules killed more VP deals than simple
>roll-over deals.

Up to a point. Thing is, we're down to 2 players, so 2 or 3 VPs have
already been awarded. This may well be a better result than the players
could have expected anyway, and so fighting it out at that stage may
well lead to a better performance for both players anyway. Will both
players be hoping to get the GW? Sure. That's a *good* thing.

>I think it is worse to have roll-over deals legal only in some
>situations and banned in others because that creates unfair situations
>like the one I presented.

What's unfair about it?

You've missed out the preceding game that led up to that point. A
player can maneuver him or herself into positions where he or she can
make beneficial deals. If they do, and get into a better position, and
execute the deal, what's unfair about that?

Just as you can be outclassed by someone with better resource management
than you, or better deck building skills than you, you can be out-
maneuvered by someone with better table manipulation skills than you.

V:TES is *not* a game in which all players will have equal opportunities
to do everything at all times, nor should it be. The personality of a
player and, by extension, the "personality" of their deck will be
reflected heavily in the opportunities that come up for them.

The point is that the structure of the game should have as much
integrity as possible. Once within that structure, players should,
will, and can do anything that's possible to win. Have we got the
perfect structure? Probably not. Is there a perfect structure?
Probably not - there's a certain matter of taste to it anyway, even if
you could find a few that everyone agreed were all 100 times better than
the other options, but then everyone disagreed as to which of the
remaining options was absolutely best.

Is providing a disincentive to random cross-table shenanigans, so that I
have to defend against two Methuselahs at once for no reason related to
my play, a good thing? A fair thing? Is preserving the distinct
motives of two Methuselahs a good thing? A fair thing? I'd say yes.
Would it be nice to find a better, simple ruling/rule that made
everything even better? Sure. But I believe that where we are now is
better than where we were.

judge to understand the previous dynamic of a table if they are only
brought over later to examine a deal. I *would* have been ousted, if I
hadn't agreed to the deal. Because I agreed to the deal, you've helped
me (or not hindered me) fixing my vampires a bit, so I could oust the
rest of the table with you. So now it looks like I'm a fairly
threatening Methuselah.

After a few turns of such, is it reasonable for a judge to determine if
I can roll over or not?

If the judge can just say "Well, the two of you have to fight it out",
and the players already know this, and it can be explained in
approximately ten words, life is simple.

No, this does not mean it always happens.)

No, it's entirely in line with the logic.

1) A player who wins can win in any way he chooses. If I can get a win
by doing this deal (where I get a table win) or this other deal
(where I get a table win in a very different way) or by not
doing a deal (where I still get a table win), I can choose any
of these options. One of them might be 5VP, one of them 3VP,
and one of them might even be 2VP (and everyone else gets 1, so
I still get a table win). I can pick any of them.

2) Deals are off when you get to 2 players. The important point here is
that I can't do things that violate play-to-win at this point
(which I used to be able to, by virtue of a legal deal).

2) does not mean that 1) does not apply. It's not a case of honouring a
deal at that point. If I have a win, I can roll over - because that's
not against play-to-win behaviour. I've won.

Distasteful? Possibly. Annoying for some players? Obviously.

But it's not illogical. You just aren't seeing the actual logic at work
here.

Note also that players do NOT have to play to maximize VPs. Players
first and foremost *always* play for the GW. Many players will also
want to maximize their VPs, as a matter of personal pride. But
maximizing VPs is what you do when you can't get the GW. If you can get
the GW, you can get the GW in any way you choose.

>> This is a better situation than before. It's not perfect. If you have
>> a better suggestion, please feel free to detail it, how it would work,
>> and what up and downsides you think it would have.

enforceable.

we've agreed even if we've not actually said it. I "just happen" to be
in a very weak position when we oust the third player, so you happen to
be able to oust me.

I didn't roll-over, but the end result was basically identical.

This is not the simple solution you present it as.

>BTW it is not corner case. I had two such deals in a tournament of
>three rounds.

Since I didn't imply that this was "corner case", I have no idea why
this is relevant.

I'd be quite happy to see a better solution, but have yet to see a
coherent one.

First MY logic. The logic of the new tournament rules is to stop VP
deals. If it is not the intended logic, it is still the result of the
tournament rules, because they actually stop 95% of VP deals. That the
5% of non stopped VP deals are the ones who are violating the
principle of the game (predator-prey- relation) is a flaw of the new
tournament rules in fulfilling their job.

including maximizing VPs. To win a toruinament you need GWs and VPs.

> As already explained by LSJ *in this thread*, this isn't particularly

Messages.Author: ben...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:
x5m...@gmx.de wrote:
> First MY logic. The logic of the new tournament rules is to stop VP
> deals. If it is not the intended logic, it is still the result of the
> tournament rules, because they actually stop 95% of VP deals. That the
> 5% of non stopped VP deals are the ones who are violating the
> principle of the game (predator-prey- relation) is a flaw of the new
> tournament rules in fulfilling their job.

And now MY logic:

That remaining 5% is not a flaw in the tournament rules, but rather
a flaw in the strategy of the players involved. Every time I see a
post to the newsgroup from someone compaining about deals being legal
or illegal, or contriving some PTW/VP-maximization situation in order
to create some universe-imploding paradox, the correct answer is that
the players involved were shortsightedly thinking that a weak position
means they should sacrifice their game to scrape a VP instead of
trying to find a way to win the game despite the poor odds. In my
experience, the best way to make the finals of a tournament is to WIN
GAMES. Yes, you'll find yourself in situations where your chances of
winning a game are poor. However, if you look beyond that one
tournament and instead look at your track record over the course of a
series of tournaments, you'll find that you'll make the final round
more often by taking the poor-odds chance of going for the win than by
taking the no chance of getting that 1 VP. Only if you know that you
have NO chance of winning the game at all should you go for the 1
VP.

This is ESPECIALLY true in the North American and European
Championships, where you KNOW you need at least 2 GW to make the
finals. If you're in Round 3 with 1 GW and you're trying to weasel
out a VP deal, you should be slapped with a handful of crepes.

> including maximizing VPs. To win a toruinament you need GWs and VPs.

Now we get to the FURTHERMORE part of MY logic.

FURTHERMORE, if you go for GW instead of VP, when you make the final
round your odds of winning are improved because you are more likely to
have the higher seed in the finals - a very advantageous position.
I'm pretty sure it has something to do with GW being the FIRST
TIEBREAKER.

Oh, and you should all play faster, too. That way you won't be
scrambling to make GW and VP deals before time runs out. Oh, and you
should all shut yer yaps, too. That way you won't waste time during
the game negotiating deals, only to see VP and GW slip away from you
as time runs out.

Play. The. Game.

Win. The. Game.

- Ben Peal
